etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English eccho, ecco, ekko, from Medieval Latin ecco, from Latin echo, from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ), from ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound”). Possibly from the same Proto-Indo-European root as sough.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) Of a sound or sound waves: to reflect off a surface and return; to reverberate or resound.

quote.citation: 1953 July, Allen Rowley, “First Impressions of American Railways”, in Railway Magazine, page 493:
quote.text: With each clap of thunder echoing from one high building to another the noise was terrific.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, figuratively) Of a rumour, opinion, etc.: to spread or reverberate.

quote.citation: 2004 October 29, Marco R. Della Cava, “Vaccine shortage pricks tempers”, in Statesman Journal, volume 152, number 214, Salem, OR, page 2A:
quote.text: The sense that it takes outrageous fortune to get inoculated echoes here in the Bay Area, where pharmacies have canceled flu-shot clinics, doctors turn away pleading patients and health officials are reduced to telling panicked callers that they should practice good personal hygiene.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Those peals are echoed by the Trojan throng.

quote.citation: 1827, John Keble, The Christian Year: Christmas Day:
quote.text: The wondrous sound / Is echoed on forever.

definitions.definition: (transitive, figuratively) To repeat (another’s speech, opinion, etc.).

quote.citation: 2013 July-August, Sarah Glaz, “Ode to Prime Numbers”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 4:
quote.text: Some poems, echoing the purpose of early poetic treatises on scientific principles, attempt to elucidate the mathematical concepts that underlie prime numbers. Others play with primes’ cultural associations. Still others derive their structure from mathematical patterns involving primes.

quote.citation: 2023 March 8, David Clough, “The long road that led to Beeching”, in RAIL, number 978, page 43:
quote.text: His views were echoed by The Economist, which feared that the effects of modernisation would be no more than “chromium-plated” inefficiency caused by unimaginative railway management and adverse union reaction.

definitions.definition: (computing, transitive) To repeat its input as input to some other device or system.

quote.citation: 1991, Martin D. Seyer, RS-232 made easy:
quote.text: The device that is to echo the characters should be optioned for echoplexing.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, whist, bridge) To give the echo signal, informing one's partner about cards one holds.
